video_title: Why 600,000 People Live On This Rock With No Resources
transcript: For many reasons, the small islands of Malta that are roughly in the center of the Mediterranean aren't where you would initially expect to find a thriving civilization at. Located roughly 93 km south of Sicily and about 288 km north of Libya, the Maltese archipelago consists of three larger main islands called Malta, Gozo, and Comino. Along with several smaller islands that collectively take up only about 316 sq km of land. This puts Malta within the top 10 smallest sovereign countries in the world today. And to help maybe put it in a perspective for you, it's less than half the total size of New York City. These small islands are also almost completely bereft of any resources that would be useful for a human settlement, let alone civilization. There are no mineral or fossil fuel resources to speak of at all. There is very limited agricultural land that would be useful for food production. And perhaps worst of all, there are practically zero obvious freshwater sources, either. There are no permanent sources of freshwater anywhere on Malta's surface. >> [music] >> No rivers, no lakes, and a dry environment with scant rainfall that falls extremely unevenly throughout the year. 3/4 of Malta's rainfall usually all just comes during the wet season between October and March. While the summers are usually all just completely rain-free for months at a time. Even worse, the islands of Malta are basically just barren limestone rocks protruding out of the sea. Which means that rainfall on them rapidly infiltrates the limestone geology deep underground or runs out to the sea instead of collecting on the surface. These islands are a very difficult to inhabit set of rocks in the middle of the salty sea. And yet, Malta is by far the most densely populated country in Europe these days regardless. And it's not even close. As of 2025, 588,000 people are believed to be living in Malta. Which gives the country an incredible population density of 1,838 people per square kilometer. That level of population density absolutely dwarfs every single other country within the EU. The EU's next most [music] densest country, the Netherlands, is only about 1/4 as dense on average as Malta is. In fact, Malta's population density is so significant that it's the fifth most densely populated country in the entire world. For mating only behind Monaco, Singapore, Vatican City, and Bahrain. If you remove the tiny city states of Monaco and Vatican City from the consideration, both of which are only a tiny fraction of the size of even Malta, then Malta is really the third most densely populated non-microstate country in the world and by far the densest one in all of Europe. To put this into a bit more perspective, Malta has a significantly larger population than Iceland does. Despite being way smaller and with substantially less resources. Iceland only has a population of 394,000 people compared to Malta's 588,000 people. Despite Iceland being more than 326 times larger than Malta is geographically. Life on Malta can feel very crowded and congested these days despite everything stacked against it. And what's even more strange is how all of this is a pretty recent phenomenon for the country. Historically, until very recently, Malta was almost always an emigrant nation where more people left than came. Over the course of just a single recent generation between 1948 and 1967, nearly a third of Malta's entire population left the country amidst chronic economic stagnation and lack of opportunity. And there are at least two known instances in Malta's history before then where the islands have been completely abandoned and depopulated altogether. So, the big question that I wanted to ask is why do so many people live on these tiny, difficult to inhabit rocks without any water or useful resources today. How was Malta able to overcome its seemingly crippling geographic handicaps to become the most densely populated country in Europe today? To begin answering these questions, we need to start with a deeper look into Malta's geography and what makes it more useful and desirable than its lack of resources and barriers to settlement when initially suggest. Malta's value has never been about what could be extracted from the island, but what could be controlled from the island. Malta is arguably the single most important geo-strategic location for any power to control in order to dominate the Mediterranean Sea other than maybe the Strait of Gibraltar and the Sea of Marmara and in more modern times the Suez Canal. It sits almost precisely in the dead center of the Mediterranean near one of the seas most important geographic funnels. Historically, before the creation of the Suez Canal, the only way for ships to travel between the western and eastern halves of the Mediterranean was either to the north or south of Sicily. Through either the very narrow Strait of Messina in the north between Sicily and the Italian mainland or through the larger gap between Sicily and modern-day Tunisia. And Malta is the most strategically placed landmass to influence and project power into that larger southern passage from. A power base placed in Malta could most easily observe, protect, raid, or threaten shipping moving between the two halves of the Mediterranean. And that alone made the possession of Malta strategically valuable. Malta also sits in the middle of Europe and North Africa, which has always made it strategically useful for powers moving in both directions. And even better, the main island of Malta itself also just happens to possess one of the finest natural harbors in the entire Mediterranean as well. The eastern side of Malta contains both the Grand Harbor and the Marsamxett Harbor separated by the large peninsula in between them where the fortified city of Valletta was eventually built in the 16th century. These harbors are deep, sheltered, extensive, and also surrounded by easily defensible terrain. The Grand Harbor, in particular, has all of these narrow peninsulas and inlets that can be covered by forts and artillery from multiple angles of defense, which make it extremely difficult for any outside attacker to just simply sail themselves into the harbor and get away with it. And this [music] excellent harbor is also on that very strategically well-placed island in the center of the Mediterranean at the entrance to that passage between Sicily and Tunisia. A fleet parked in this harbor around Valletta in Malta could have an easy-to-defend base to operate throughout the entire Mediterranean from, as well as an outpost to control the movement of trade and enemy naval forces from passing between both halves of the Mediterranean, too. It is basically a pre-made naval fortress in the heart of the Mediterranean. And that has made it an extremely attractive place to be controlled by empires for thousands of years now. Throughout ancient and medieval history, the island was controlled at various different times by the Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Normans, Arabs, and Spanish for this very reason. But its strategic importance reached an all-time high during the 16th century when it became a major target of conquest by the Ottoman Empire. The Knights Hospitaller, or the Knights of St. John, was granted sovereignty by the Holy Roman Empire to rule over Malta in 1530 and to defend it against the expanding Ottomans. The Knights were able to use Malta as a heavily militarized outpost in the center of the Mediterranean to raid Ottoman shipping from and to block any Ottoman expansion from reaching into the western Mediterranean or southern Italy. So, naturally, the Ottomans came to view Malta as a major obstacle to their expansion. And so, in 1565, they sent an armada with tens of thousands of men to try and conquer the island. But despite outnumbering the defending Knights on the island by as many as eight to one, they still failed to overcome Malta's defenses and nearly the entire attacking Ottoman force was destroyed. The control of Malta by the Christian powers in the 16th century is effectively what prevented the Ottomans from expanding into the Western Mediterranean. And it wouldn't be the last time that Malta's strategic geography would affect regional geopolitics. Napoleon recognized Malta's strategic geography during his time as well. During his expedition to Egypt in 1798, he managed to succeed where the Ottomans had failed in conquering Malta from the knights along the way in order to protect his own sea lines of communication and logistics between Egypt and the French mainland. It didn't last for long though, because the islanders rose up in a revolt against the French quickly thereafter. And then the British arrived in 1800 to help kick the French out. And as the British so often did in their history, they ended up just staying around afterward and controlled Malta for the next 164 years well into the 1960s. To the British, Malta became one of their most strategically located overseas possessions. They transformed it into a fortress and refueling depot for the Royal Navy in the center of the Mediterranean. And it became the centerpiece in their chain of outposts on the way to India that ran from the British mainland through Gibraltar and Malta and the Suez Canal. And then, Malta's geo-strategic importance became extremely acute again during the Second World War. After Italy entered the war on the side of the Axis, British-controlled Malta sat immediately in between Sicily and Italian-controlled Libya. Malta was therefore a perfectly positioned base for the British to use to attack Axis supply lines running between Europe and North Africa from. An unsinkable aircraft carrier and submarine base deep behind enemy lines that once again turned Malta into the object of a relentless campaign to conquer it. Between 1940 and 1942, the Axis subjected Malta to a massive bombing campaign that attempted to starve the island out through blockade, while the British went to truly extraordinary lengths to keep the island supplied and in the fight. So, Malta's always been very useful for outside powers to control or influence from a strategic perspective, which has always meant that there have been powerful empires willing to bankroll the island's settlement and development. But, the biggest problem standing in their way has always been that Malta has basically zero obvious sources of fresh water or resources that would be necessary to sustain that settlement or development. So, how have the people in Malta managed to do it anyway? For most of Malta's history, the strategy of conserving water was pretty basic. The general rule was that whenever it rained, as much of it as possible was to be captured. Homes, villas, farms, and public buildings all across the island came to incorporate underground cisterns. Well, rain falling on rooftops and courtyards was channeled towards them. By the medieval period, most houses in Malta had these kinds of underground cisterns built into their architecture. And while Malta has no permanent sources of fresh water anywhere on its surface, there are limited quantities of groundwater beneath its surface that are roughly divided into two different kinds of groundwater. Perched aquifers in the western parts of Malta that are geographically situated higher up than sea level, and lower elevated sea level aquifers. Historically, the more highly elevated perched aquifers had more limited supplies of groundwater, but their shallower depth than the sea level aquifers made them relatively easier to reach. Nonetheless, because rainfall is scant and largely seasonal in Malta, the availability of water was always a chronic issue on the islands until the modern era. After the Ottomans laid siege to Malta and failed to capture it in 1565, the Knights of St. John began the construction of the fortified city of Valletta on that peninsula that separates the Grand Harbor from the Marsamxett Harbor on the island. Well aware of the lack of water in this area, however, and nervous about another siege, the Knights mandated that every single home and building in Valletta needed to have a well or cistern, while gardens were explicitly forbidden in order to conserve even more water. After the city continued growing and the Knights realized that rainwater and limited groundwater wasn't going to be enough to sustain it, they began building Malta's first major aqueduct in 1610. When it was finished in 1615, the aqueduct began delivering water to Valletta from a spring up on higher ground about 27 km away that was enough to supply all of the city's freshwater needs until the 19th century, when the population began growing dramatically. After the British took over Malta's political affairs in 1800, they eventually introduced the island's first motorized pumps and were the first ones to actually exploit the island's larger and deeper sea-level aquifers in an organized manner. The British introduced industrial water storage and exploitation to the islands with huge underground reservoirs, pumping stations, and pipelines. They constructed a series of small dams in one of the valleys of Malta to collect rainfall in a reservoir called the Chadwick Lakes. And they even experimented with a very early form of seawater desalination in Malta all the way back in the 1880s that attempted to boil seawater and condense the resulting vapor. While the technology worked at the time, it was also far too energy intensive to ever be economically viable. The dream was there to eventually take advantage of the fact that Malta was literally surrounded by water, just the wrong kind of water, but it wouldn't become economically viable until the advent of modern reverse osmosis desalination nearly a century later in the 1960s. During the Second World War between 1940 and 1942, when Malta was besieged by the Axis powers, the island came dangerously close to simply running out of water entirely. The Axis bombing campaign of Malta deliberately targeted the island's pumping stations, water mains, electricity infrastructure, and reservoirs. And by early 1941, the island's water service had already been put out of action. Water began to be rationed, but water delivery on Malta was forced to improvise with water carts and tanks hidden beneath rocks for protection. Even though the Axis siege was broken by the Allies over the summer of 1942, it showed how vulnerable Malta still was to water supply issues even in the 20th century. >> [music] >> And the situation would arguably get even worse just a few decades later in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Following the end of the Second World War, rapid population growth, economic development, plumbing, tourism, and agriculture all caused water consumption in Malta to skyrocket. For a few decades, Malta dealt with this simply by pumping up more of its ground water. But like all other aquifers around the world, they weren't bottomless. The aquifers beneath Malta are formed through decades of rainfall slowly percolating beneath the surface, and they can't be replenished very quickly. If fresh water gets removed from the aquifers faster than rainfall can replenish it, salty sea water lying beneath the fresh water layer will start to infiltrate it, which is exactly what started happening in Malta by the late 1970s. Groundwater production began to be forced to slow down, and water rationing once again returned back to Malta. The natural water supply on Malta had reached its maximum demand capacity. And in order to grow any further, the island needed a brand new source of water to add to its supply mix. And luckily for Malta, this was about at the exact same time the reverse osmosis desalination was starting to become really economically feasible. Rather than boiling sea water and condensing the vapor, reverse osmosis forces the water under enormous pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass through while rejecting dissolved solids. In 1983, Malta finally opened what was at the time the largest reverse osmosis plant in the world at Għar Lapsi. And with it, the island initiated a revolution in its water supply. For the first time in Malta's history, the amount of available potable water wasn't strictly defined by the island's rainfall. Malta was finally able to connect itself to an inexhaustible raw water reservoir, the Mediterranean Sea itself. And additional reverse osmosis plants quickly followed. Today, roughly 70% of Malta's water supply comes through reverse osmosis desalination, while the remaining 30% still comes up from groundwater, which makes Malta by far the most desalination-dependent country in Europe today, and the most desalination-dependent anywhere in the world outside of the Middle East. And today, much like throughout Malta's history, there are still fears that the islands are approaching the point of overpopulation. We now know from archaeological evidence that Malta has been inhabited since at least around 6500 BC. But we also know that Malta appears to have been abruptly abandoned for decades sometime around 2500 BC, perhaps because of water supply issues. The next time that Malta appears to have been largely abandoned in the historical record was after the Arab conquest of the islands in 870 AD, which was such a devastating event that the islands remained practically uninhabited for nearly the next 180 years until 1048, when they were resettled again by other Arabs who came from Sicily, which is why the Maltese language today is a Semitic language that's closely related to Arabic and somewhat mutually intelligible with the Arabic that's still spoken today in Tunisia and Libya. Throughout most of Malta's history, before and after both of these periods of abandonment, the population was never remotely as large as it's become today. Just a little more than 500 years ago in the 15th century, Malta's population wasn't even more than 20,000 people. And yet its rulers still believed at that time that it was probably too many. The last time in Malta's history that the islands produced a surplus of wheat and barley was all the way back sometime around 1437. From 1440 onwards, and even more so after 1480, Malta began importing larger and larger amounts of food from beyond the islands in order to sustain themselves, especially from nearby Sicily, which led to widespread concerns of overpopulation on the islands. Before the Knights of St. John took charge of Malta in 1530, they conducted a commission which reported that Malta was a sterile, arid, rocky island that couldn't provide enough food for even its own population for any more than just 4 months out of the year. By 1632, when the Knights conducted a census in Malta to determine how much food they needed to import from Sicily, they discovered that the island's population by then stood at a little more than 45,000 people, more than double the number since they had arrived to the islands a century earlier. Nearly three centuries later, when the British conducted their own census in Malta in 1901, they found that the population had climbed to more than 184,000 people, which the British government believed was unsustainable and which also gave Malta the highest population density anywhere in the world at the time. In 1964, when Malta gained its independence from Britain, the new Maltese government explicitly identified overpopulation as one of the new country's biggest problems to deal with, along with a lack of job and wealth creation to provide a good enough life for the island's residents. Between 1948 and 1967, as Malta's economy stagnated and overpopulation pressures intensified, nearly a third of the entire island's population simply packed up their bags and left to find better economic opportunities elsewhere, lending Malta a historical legacy of an immigrating nation, much like Ireland. Nonetheless, by the turn of the 21st century, Malta's population had swelled to roughly 400,000 people. And in only the 26 years since then, it swelled even further to more than 588,000 people. And it's projected to reach more than 630,000 people by the end of this decade in 2030. By that point, Malta's population density will be approaching 2,000 people per square kilometer. And it'll likely surpass Bahrain's population density to become the second most densely populated non-microstate country in the world, only behind Singapore. And what's truly remarkable is the local indigenous Maltese people are not the ones who've been driving any of this population growth at all. Their birth rate has been continually collapsing for decades now, >> [music] >> to the point where it's now among the absolute lowest in the world today. The last time that Malta's fertility rate was at the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman was all the way back in 1975. And it's declined every single decade since then, to the point where currently stands at just 1.06 children per woman today, which is the lowest birth rate in Europe outside of Ukraine and Vatican City, and the seventh lowest measured in the world. And it's even worse for indigenous Maltese women whose own fertility rate has fallen all the way to just 0.7 children per woman right now, which is even lower than the lowest fertility rate in the world in South Korea, which currently stands at 0.76 children per woman. And yet, Malta is also Europe's fastest growing country at the same time, having gained 47% in its population just since the start [music] of the century in 2000. And that's because Malta's modern population explosion has been entirely driven by immigration from abroad rather than by local births. As recently as 2015, only 10% of Malta's population were born abroad outside of the islands. But then, within just 10 years by 2025, that ratio had more than tripled to roughly 31% of Malta's population be foreign-born, which is now the highest ratio of any country in Europe other than microstates and Luxembourg. And more are still coming with every passing year. Just between the summers of 2025 and 2026 alone, Malta's population grew by 2.4% year over year. By far the highest growth rate seen anywhere on the European continent that was nearly double the next highest growth rate of 1.3% that was seen in Luxembourg. [music] As far back as 2014, Malta's government spoke openly about emulating the economic growth model of Dubai on the islands by encouraging unprecedented immigration from abroad. And as recently as June of 2023, Malta's finance minister stated plainly that the country's population should increase to 800,000 strong by 2040. By 2050, if current projections hold, it has been estimated that two out of every three workers in Malta will be foreign-born. People from all walks of life and from all around the world are attracted to move to Malta for a variety of reasons. The country has been a part of the EU since 2004, which opened up relatively easy migration to Malta from the rest of the EU for people seeking warmer weather, lower taxes, and a population that is overwhelmingly fluent in English because of the long history of British colonial rule. Malta's top personal income tax rate tops out at just 35%, which isn't the lowest rate in the EU, but it's still significantly lower than in countries like Germany, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, or Sweden, which in addition to the warm climate and the English language proficiency has made it an attractive place to relocate to for mobile high-income individuals from these other countries. It's also increasingly an attractive place for internationally mobile foreign companies to relocate to, as well, because of Malta's unique corporate tax structure. Malta officially charges a relatively high 35% corporate tax rate, but there's a major loophole built in where active trading profits that are distributed to a holding company allow for a 6/7 refund of all the corporate tax paid. This means that in reality, the final net corporate tax rate the companies actually end up paying in Malta is only 5%, a fraction of most other countries. For example, in the UK, the corporate tax rate is a firm 25% without any loopholes like this, which means that a UK-based company that relocates to Malta can save huge amounts of money on their corporate tax bill, and they'll also be in a much warmer, sunnier country where everybody still speaks English anyway. In 2025, Sky Bet, which used to be a major UK-based online gambling company, made headlines when they relocated their headquarters to Malta for exactly these reasons, and they'll almost certainly not be the last large UK company to do so. The population of millionaires in Malta grew by an astonishing 74% over just 10 years between 2013 to 2023 for all of these reasons. But normal everyday people are moving to Malta in large numbers as well in search of work in the booming construction, hospitality, and tourism industries. Tourism, especially, is one of the largest industries and economic drivers in Malta that has been continually growing larger and larger across the 21st century, which contributes to the island's feeling even more densely populated than their raw population numbers alone would suggest. As recently as 2000, Malta only received about 1.2 million tourists throughout the year. But only a quarter of a century later in 2025, Malta received more than 4 million tourists, nearly quadruple the number who had visited back in 2000. Based on a per capita metric of foreign tourist nights spent per 1,000 residents, Malta is now the third most heavily visited non-microstate country in Europe, remaining only just barely behind Croatia and Iceland. During the peak of the summer travel season, Malta's actual population includes roughly 110,000 tourists at any given time, which means that Malta's summertime population already swells to as many as 700,000 people when all of the tourists are included as well, which only makes Malta feel even more dense. Tourism and hospitality, along with the low taxes that are attracting foreign companies and millionaires, make up a substantial part of the Maltese economy today, and they're the major driver of the island's explosive population growth during the 21st century as well. But they're also causing Malta's cost of living to explode at the same time, and it's arguably harming the quality of life for the average local Maltese person, too. The average asking price for an apartment in Malta has soared to 414,000 euros as of 2026, almost 10% higher than it was just the year previously in 2025, and roughly 16 times the average Maltese annual income. For reference, in the US, the price of an average house is only about 3 and 1/2 times the average American annual income. So, the housing affordability crisis in Malta is about 4 and 1/2 times worse than it is in America. And then, there's the matter of traffic and congestion with all of these people and tourists to consider in Malta as well. You might expect that the most densely populated country in Europe with more than four times the density of the Netherlands would have a robust public transportation and metro system. But, Malta, in fact, doesn't even have a single operational railway or metro at all. All public transportation on the islands is conducted entirely by bus and ferry, and most people just drive everywhere themselves. Practically all transportation in Malta shares the exact same road network, which makes Malta feel extremely congested with traffic basically all of the time. There are about 440,000 motor vehicles that are currently registered in Malta, which gives it one of the highest densities of vehicles anywhere on the planet. Malta averages 1,392 motor vehicles per square kilometer right now, which is even more than Singapore, [music] a literal city-state which averages 1,338 motor vehicles per square kilometer. As a result, what was once a calm, peaceful island in the Mediterranean appears to increasingly look more and more like a giant car park these days. And in addition to the traffic and the rising housing prices, many Maltese increasingly fear the loss of their identity that could accompany all of this immigration as well. The Maltese language itself is an incredibly unique gem of a language that is entirely a product of these islands' unique history. It is the only Semitic language in the world that is written in the Latin alphabet. Its speakers invoke the word Allah whenever they pray to God while being an overwhelmingly Roman Catholic people. It is still somewhat mutually intelligible with Arabic speakers in nearby Tunisia and Libya, and it is the only Semitic language that is indigenous in the EU. The Maltese, understandably, desire to safeguard the unique heritage of their language. But how much can they manage to do that in this era of globalization, where the local indigenous Maltese fertility rate is already among the lowest in the world because of the island's cost of living crisis, [music] where Malta's population is already nearly 1/3 foreign-born and might reach more than 40% foreign-born by 2050, and on top of all of the millions of non-Maltese speaking tourists who visit the islands every year? Malta's economy and population both might well continue growing substantially further during the 21st century. But to what end? Does the average Maltese person experience a better quality of life today with all of the increased density and the larger economy than their parents or their grandparents did? The answer to that question is very far from clear, as is the direction of Malta's future.
